reception.text: The Luquillo reserve barely registered on the mainland; the only wire story that mentioned it was about gold in the island's streams, not forestry.

political_impact.text: The proclamation reserved only unclaimed public land inside a boundary of about 65,950 acres; Gifford estimated the federal forest land at about 20,000 acres.
political_impact.source: Gifford, USDA Bureau of Forestry Bulletin 54 (1905), p. 9

legacy.text: A survey in 1916 found about 12,400 acres of federal land in the reserve.
Luquillo became the Caribbean National Forest in 1935 and the El Yunque National Forest in 2007, the only tropical rainforest in the National Forest System.
El Yunque is a refuge for the Puerto Rican parrot, federally listed as endangered since March 11, 1967, and still holds a small wild flock.
legacy.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, ECOS species record

today.name: El Yunque National Forest
today.note: The only tropical rainforest in the National Forest System.

related.note: Made under the same Act of July 1, 1902, reserving public lands in Puerto Rico.
Made under the same Act of July 1, 1902, reserving public lands in Puerto Rico.

later_actions.text: Became the Luquillo National Forest when Congress renamed all forest reserves national forests.
Renamed the El Yunque National Forest by executive order, not by Congress.

uncertain: Exactly how much land the proclamation reserved is uncertain: the boundary enclosed about 65,950 acres, but only unclaimed public land inside it was reserved.

political_impact.text: The proclamation superseded the Yellowstone and Teton reserves in Wyoming and the Absaroka in Montana and set up one Yellowstone Forest Reserve in their place.
On May 4, 1904, Roosevelt redrew the reserve, cutting 518,600 acres.

legacy.text: The reserve was divided on July 1, 1908, among the Targhee, Teton, Wyoming, Bonneville, Absaroka, Shoshone and Beartooth forests.

related.note: Redrew the reserve in 1904, cutting 518,600 acres.

reception.text: The Salt Lake Herald ran the Gunnison and Mayfield petition under the headline "RIGHTS OF PEOPLE AS AGAINST SHEEP."
The Deseret Evening News reported the claim that the federal order would cause the destruction of 200,000 sheep.
The Salt Lake Tribune headlined the raised grazing limit "AN EXCELLENT COMPROMISE."

political_impact.text: By early February 1904 Sanpete County wool growers met in convention at Manti and cattlemen at Ephraim; Gunnison and Mayfield petitioned for the water of Twelve Mile Creek, and Manti residents sent a counter-petition.
After Senators Reed Smoot and Thomas Kearns intervened, Smoot going to Pinchot personally, Interior raised the grazing limit from 175,000 head to 300,000.

legacy.text: The La Sal National Forest was abolished and joined to the Manti in 1949, and the combined forest was renamed Manti-La Sal in 1950.

today.name: Manti-La Sal National Forest
today.note: The only hyphenated national forest that is a single proclaimed forest.

later_actions.text: La Sal National Forest lands transferred to the Manti.
Combined forest renamed Manti-La Sal National Forest.

uncertain: The full size of the Manti grazing fight may be larger than the surviving record shows, since Salt Lake papers of the period are hard to read in digitized form.

legacy.text: Logan was combined with about 500,000 more acres into the Bear River Forest Reserve in 1906; the eastern part of the Bear River became the Cache National Forest in 1908, and the Utah portion went to today's Uinta-Wasatch-Cache after 1973.

related.note: Bear River Forest Reserve created in place of the Logan, with about 500,000 more acres.
Abolished the Bear River and created the Cache National Forest from its eastern part.

later_actions.text: The Cache National Forest was split; the Utah portion holding the original Logan lands went to what is now the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache.

political_impact.text: The proclamation superseded both the 1897 Lewis and Clarke reserve and the 1897 Flathead reserve.

related.note: The 1907 proclamation that dropped the final "e" from Clarke.

later_actions.text: The Helena and Lewis and Clark National Forests were administratively combined.

reception.text: A syndicated survey of Idaho protest against reserves exempted Pocatello, saying it was "to protect the water supply of Pocatello and a necessity existed for its creation."

political_impact.text: A September 1903 wire story reported a federal suit against southeastern Idaho stockmen, including a sitting state senator, for grazing 28,000 sheep on the Portneuf headwaters and fouling Pocatello's water.

legacy.text: The Pocatello was abolished in 1915 and its lands moved to the Cache, then on to the Caribou in 1939 and 1942.

related.note: Created the Caribou Forest Reserve, which later received the old Pocatello lands.

later_actions.text: Pocatello National Forest abolished and its lands moved to the Cache, effective July 1, 1915.
Pocatello and Portneuf divisions moved to the Caribou National Forest.
Malad division moved to the Caribou National Forest.

reception.text: The Salt Lake Tribune reported that people living on and near the Aquarius reserve were "well satisfied with the reserve."

legacy.text: Renamed the Powell National Forest in 1908, it was abolished in 1944–45 and all 1,056,278 gross acres joined to the Dixie, which still has a Powell Ranger District.

today.name: Dixie National Forest
today.note: The northern part of the old Aquarius Plateau lands is managed by the neighboring Fishlake.

later_actions.text: Powell National Forest abolished, effective October 1, 1944, and its lands made part of the Dixie.

legacy.text: Payson merged into the Nebo National Forest in 1908; in 1915 the Mount Nebo unit, which held the 1903 addition, went to the Uinta.

related.note: Merged the Payson into the Nebo National Forest.

later_actions.text: Nebo National Forest abolished and its lands sent to the Manti.
Mount Nebo unit, holding Roosevelt's 1903 addition, given to the Uinta with an earlier effective date than the executive order.

reception.text: A petition asking that a supervisor be appointed for the Highwood Mountains reserve was "being generously signed."

legacy.text: Combined into the Jefferson National Forest of Montana in 1908; that forest was abolished in 1932 and its lands moved to the Lewis and Clark. The Highwood Mountains are still listed among its ranges.

related.note: Combined the Highwood Mountains into the Jefferson National Forest (Montana).

later_actions.text: Jefferson National Forest (Montana) abolished and its 1,174,804 gross acres transferred to the Lewis and Clark.

reception.text: The Santa Barbara Morning Press greeted the signing as insuring "For All Time A Sufficient Water Supply For This City."
The Los Angeles Herald called the added ranch the principal watershed of the Santa Ynez River, from which Santa Barbara hoped to draw a permanent water supply.
The Ventura Daily Post noted the new Santa Barbara Forest Reserve.

political_impact.text: The reserve was a local campaign won: Senator Thomas R. Bard and others had worked for over two years to bring the Rancho Los Prietos y Najalayegua watershed into the reserves.
The proclamation consolidated the Pine Mountain and Zaca Lake reserve of 1898 and the Santa Ynez reserve of 1899.

legacy.text: The Santa Barbara National Forest was renamed Los Padres in 1936.

later_actions.text: Renamed the Los Padres National Forest.

uncertain: The terms of the land exchange for the Rancho Los Prietos y Najalayegua are known only from press reports, not from the proclamation.

reception.text: The 1903 forest reserves drew little national notice: no editorial engagement, eastern-paper argument or congressional-debate coverage turned up for any of them.

political_impact.text: In February 1905 the reserves passed from the General Land Office to the Forest Service.

legacy.text: All ten reserves survive inside today's national forests; most modern hyphenated forest names are administrative combinations of forests that remain separately proclaimed.
